entries.detail: The board's pinch gesture also claimed one-finger pans and consumed them, so the column above and below the board scrolled while the board itself felt frozen - whether or not the lock was on. Pinch is now two fingers only: a single finger reaches the scroll untouched, a pinch still zooms, and lifting one finger mid-pinch no longer lets the remaining finger jump the board by half a screen.

entries.title: Export at up to 4K, with the size shown before you share
entries.detail: The export sheet now offers 1080p, 2K and 4K, with 4K selected by default, and prints the exact pixel size of the file you are about to make. The renderer scales artwork, text and strokes by the same factor, streams posters in small batches and releases each one after it is drawn, so a 300-title board no longer has to hold every cover at once - and a device that cannot allocate the requested size steps down to a smaller complete image instead of failing. Score badges and the faded title band on each cover are in the file now too, so the export matches the board it came from.

entries.title: Covers stay square at every zoom
entries.detail: A tile's corner used to be a fixed 12dp, which is a rounded square at 100% and very nearly a circle on a 25dp tile at the 35% zoom floor - the peeled look of the overview. The radius is now a share of the tile's width in all three renderers, so a zoomed-out board reads as a wall of posters, the tray matches it, and an exported PNG or SVG rounds the same corners as the screen.

entries.title: Smaller motion and clarity fixes across the board
entries.detail: The drop marker springs into place instead of appearing fully formed, the lock icon and the zoom control colours animate between states, and the legend and shelf header crossfade rather than swapping text in one frame. Image elements in the SVG export are clipped to the tile, so their corners are rounded for the first time, and the export measures its output off the main thread so opening the sheet does not stutter on a large list.

entries.title: Comments and title pages no longer close the app
entries.detail: Opening a comment thread or an anime's page could force-stop when the network layer threw instead of answering with a failure, when a title page drew a row with a repeated list key, or when a theme colour could not be saved while the sheet opened. Those now surface where they belong: the comment sheet's own error row with Try again, the broken-heart status, or the summary the title page was already showing. A synopsis or comment with malformed markup is drawn as plain text rather than taking its screen down with it, and a failed title fetch leaves the page usable and able to try again.

entries.title: The AniList check says when the check itself failed
entries.detail: A reachability check from Settings that throws instead of answering used to look exactly like one that was still running. It now shows a toast with the bad news, keeps the dialog open, and leaves Check again ready - and a retry that fails the same way says so again rather than going quiet.

entries.title: The board can be narrowed by genre and by studio
entries.detail: The filter sheet now lists every genre on your list, and has a Studio section that is off until you switch it on. Studios are sorted by how many titles in your library each one made, so the ones you watch most come first. Opening the section and selecting nothing shows every studio; selections are kept while the section is off, so flipping it back on restores them rather than silently forgetting. The board and the unranked shelf use the same filters, and the sheet scrolls when a long studio list would otherwise run off the bottom.

entries.title: The whole tier list exports as one image
entries.detail: Export from the board's floating toolbar, then share the PNG or save it to Pictures/AniSequel. It renders every tier and every ranked poster at a fixed 1080-unit width - a single image rather than a screenshot of whatever fits on screen - and keeps the current genre and studio filters. Missing posters fall back to a filled tile instead of failing the export, and very large boards are scaled to stay within a safe bitmap size.

entries.title: Zoom goes down to 35%, and the board can be locked
entries.detail: The zoom range is 35-200% now, enough to see a few hundred titles on one screen. A magnifier in the app bar opens a zoom sheet with a slider and presets, the bottom stepper is smaller, and tapping its percentage resets to 100%. The lock toggle - in the stepper and the zoom sheet - turns off long-press tile dragging so a pinch is no longer taken by the drag gesture. Captions and score badges disappear below 60% instead of overflowing their tiles, and tier labels shrink to fit the narrower gutter.

entries.title: A calmer top bar and safer empty states
entries.detail: The Tiers action is an icon now, which gives the list's own name room on a 360dp screen. Titles whose cached list entry predates the genre and studio fields, posters that fail to load, and a list with no studio credits all render as empty sections or placeholder tiles instead of a null lookup. The filter and zoom sheets bound their height and scroll, so a long list of options cannot push the close action off the display.

entries.title: The tier board opens on what you have actually watched
entries.detail: A tier list is a judgement, and the longest list most people keep is the planning list - titles nobody has scored, that no drag can rank against anything. Planning is hidden by default now, and a filter sheet switches list statuses (watching, rewatching, completed, paused, dropped, planning) and airing statuses (releasing, finished, not yet aired, hiatus, cancelled) independently. Filters apply to the board and the unranked shelf together, so a hidden title cannot be dropped into a tier by accident, and the header keeps the totals while a notice says how many titles the filters are holding back. Nothing is deleted, and "Show everything" puts it all back in one tap.

entries.title: Undo and redo, both on the board
entries.detail: Undo existed; redo did not, which made an undo a decision you had to be sure about. Both now sit in a floating toolbar at the bottom of the board, within reach of the hand that made the drop, with the label of the last edit in the header. A new edit clears the redo stack - once you change something else, the branch you undid away from is no longer the future of the list - and both stacks are cleared when you switch lists.

entries.title: Tiers carry a rating band you can edit
entries.detail: Ranking from AniList scores used to read six bands from a fixed table, so a custom tier could never have one and editing a standard tier's meaning changed nothing. The band lives on the tier now and is edited from the tier manager: a 0-100 score floor on a five-point grid, or no band at all. A band of zero accepts every scored title; no band accepts none, so a tier you added but have not given a meaning to stays empty instead of collecting strays.

entries.title: Tier colours are editable
entries.detail: The coloured square in the tier manager is now the colour control. It opens a twelve-colour palette - the standard six plus six that are still legible under white text - and a recoloured tier keeps its id, so nothing filed under it moves. A newly added tier walks the same palette instead of arriving as another identical grey row.

entries.title: Zoom works like a spreadsheet
entries.detail: Pinch to zoom still works, and now there is a stepper for it: out, the percentage, in. The range is 75% to 200%, a press moves a quarter of it, and tapping the percentage resets to 100%. Zoom is per list and remembered, so a cover-only board at 180% comes back that way, and the posters and their rows are laid out from the same geometry at every level.

entries.title: Titles can move onto the cover, or go away
entries.detail: A display sheet turns names off entirely or moves them from under each poster onto its top edge, over a scrim that fades into the artwork. The layout stops reserving a caption band when there is no caption under it, so a cover-only board closes the gap instead of leaving a strip of empty background under every poster, and the score badge moves out of the name's way.

entries.title: The board has more room and a bigger drop target
entries.detail: Rows are taller, posters are wider and the gap between them is larger, so a three-across grid at 360dp is comfortable to read and to hit. The tier rows themselves are the drop targets - the row under the finger highlights before the release - and the drag ghost keeps the poster's size while the board scrolls underneath it.

entries.title: The same title opens the same page on every tab
entries.detail: A pinned title, an activity row, a library entry and a studio's filmography opened through four separate detail stores, so the same show could arrive as two different pages - and a title the Library had already loaded was fetched again from a profile. They share one store now, which means the same synopsis, cast, specs and "My Entry" tab wherever the tap came from, and leaving a tab no longer throws away what was already fetched. The pinned favourites also carry their media type now: without it a pinned manga asked AniList for the bare id, which resolves against both anime and manga and can answer with the anime sharing that number, and the sheet then refused to merge the answer - so a profile's favourites opened with no synopsis at all while the same titles opened correctly from the Library.

entries.title: Pinned characters and staff open in the app
entries.detail: The faces in a profile's Favourite Characters and Favourite Staff rows used to hand the tap to the AniList website, so the same person opened a sheet from a title's cast row and a browser page from a profile. They now open the same in-app profile sheet everywhere, with the browser kept as the fallback for a host that has no session to fetch a profile with.

entries.title: The quick-add hold has a shape, not just a colour
entries.detail: Tapping the quick-add control plans a title; holding it fills toward Currently Watching. The fill was the only sign the hold was working - the button kept the same outline the whole way - so the one gesture that means something different from a tap looked like a tap until the colour had changed. It now rounds from a rounded rectangle into a capsule as the hold completes and springs back out on release. The app's primary button does the same under a finger: it rests as a rounded square and becomes a capsule while pressed, and stays one while a request is in flight.

entries.title: The Info page counts down once
entries.detail: The progress card printed "airs in in 3d" - the countdown already returns its own preposition - and described a manga as airing episodes. A manga now says "Chapter 12 publishes in 3d", and a title with no progress card of its own gets a "Next episode" or "Next chapter" line in the specs card instead, so the date is in one place or the other, never both and never missing.

entries.title: Long Info rows scroll, and copying says so
entries.detail: The sheet behind a meta row's "..." now scrolls when the list is longer than the sheet, and its chevron points down to say so instead of sideways. Copying a title confirms it in place - the icon turns into a check and the row tints - rather than leaving the reader to guess whether the tap registered.

entries.title: The joke toast rises instead of falling
entries.detail: It is anchored to the bottom of the screen, and it used to animate in from above - so the one surface meant to feel like the app raising a remark read as the bar dropping it. It rises from the bar now, grows out of its own bottom edge, and leaves the way it came. The glyph it was wearing is the app's update-available mark, the same one on the update dialog, so it now wears the sparkle instead; it sits a little higher off a busy page; and it is announced to a screen reader, which it never was - a surface that appears by itself used to be completely silent.

entries.title: The empty state stops breathing in the background
entries.detail: The morphing orb behind an empty page kept its animation running for as long as the screen was composed, which includes the whole time the app was in the background. It draws one static shape while the app is not on screen and starts the clock again when it is. Same orb, no frames spent on a screen nobody is looking at.

entries.title: Typing in the search box no longer repaints the whole app
entries.detail: Every dashboard update replaced the state the app's root was reading, so each character typed into the filter box recomposed the navigation host, the bar and the toast just to find out that nothing had changed. The viewer and the home-screen widget inputs are derived now, and the widget sync runs in a scope of its own, so a keystroke redraws only what actually moved.

entries.title: Profile and Library load again
entries.detail: AniList quietly broke four fields in the profile query. Asking for any one of them made the whole request fail with a server error, so the Profile and Library pages showed "Ani-chan is having a nap" while Home - which uses a different query - kept working. The charts now read the same numbers from the block AniList actually maintains: formats, release years, genres and tags, all populated again.

entries.title: Your list is there before the network is
entries.detail: Opening the app now paints the copy already on your device first, then refreshes behind it. If AniList does not answer, that copy stays instead of being replaced by a failure page, with a small "Saved copy" pill so a day-old list never pretends to be a live one. Home, Profile and Library all do this, and a saved copy up to thirty days old is still considered yours to read.

entries.title: A library icon that looks like a library
entries.detail: The Library tab was borrowing the Stats tab's stopwatch, which read as time watched and made two different destinations share one glyph. It is now the app's own shelf-of-books vector, drawn in the same style as the rest of the icon set.

entries.title: No more empty stat charts
entries.detail: Format, genre, tag and release-year distributions are read from the modern statistics block, which returns real tallies for real accounts. The Stats tab and the demo both draw from the same shape, so the fixture can no longer pass while the live request fails.

entries.title: The Library and profile pull their own weight
entries.detail: The Library grid now refreshes with the pull gesture instead of sending you back to Home to refresh there, the bar above it says how many titles are in the list, and the profile finally has a refresh control - its refresh bar existed but nothing could start it. The profile's title crossfades from "Profile" to the account name instead of reading "AniList" while it loads, and the Saved copy pill springs in and out rather than snapping on the line above the content.

entries.title: Twenty-three more ways for Ani-chan to be asleep
entries.detail: The failure pool gained another twenty-three lines - a coma arc, a container that restarted with the plot, a health check answering "lol" - plus four new rate-limit lines and twelve more ambient jokes for the toast above the bar.

entries.title: The API check no longer takes over your own pages
entries.detail: 1.5.1 put the whole AniList failure scene - the broken heart, the status strip, the joke and the "go touch grass" exit - on the Profile and Library pages, where it arrived over content you had been reading a second earlier and buried the retry button under a screenful of theatre. Those two pages now say what happened, make one joke and offer the two honest exits; the scene stays where you went looking for it, on the dashboard's error screen and the Settings connection check.

entries.title: The heartbreak got a better performance
entries.detail: The heart now beats twice, the second time harder, then shivers and compresses before it gives. The crack itself throws a shockwave with debris flying out of the seam, and the halves part on a bouncy spring, sink with their own weight and settle. It is still the same two vector halves coming apart and the same green glue stitching them back together, just with the beat and the brace that make it read as a heart failing instead of a shape being pulled apart.

entries.title: Twenty more ways for Ani-chan to be asleep
entries.detail: The down pool gained twenty lines - a Friday deploy, a beach episode, a flashback arc, a dropped database that bounced twice, a Wi-Fi isekai and a cron job crying in production - for sixty-eight in total. A retry loop now also lands on a *new* joke each time: the seed was derived from the failure's own text, which is identical on every retry of the same failure, so the pool had been handing you the same line every time you tapped Try again.

entries.title: A joke now and then, from nowhere
entries.detail: Every few minutes, while you are on Home, Library or your own Profile, a small card slides down above the bar with a line about backlogs, recaps and rewatches. It waits between four and fifteen minutes (the first one comes sooner), stays for five seconds, and leaves on a tap. It never appears over the login screen, Settings or a title sheet, and it stops the moment the app goes to the background.

entries.title: The Check button always answers
entries.detail: Tapping Check while a check was already running did nothing at all - the tap was dropped rather than queued - so the strip showed the answer to a request you did not make. A tap is now queued and runs as soon as the current request lands. A check that could not produce a verdict no longer draws the broken heart and "Ani-chan is confused" in Settings; it says the question is unanswered and offers to ask again. And a probe whose request threw no longer leaves the strip checking forever.

entries.title: When AniList is down, Ani-chan is sleeping
entries.detail: A failed load no longer says "connection error" and leaves you guessing. Every failure now names what actually happened - no signal, a rate limit, an expired session, a server taking a nap - in a sentence you can act on, with one of forty-plus jokes underneath. A new status strip asks AniList with a tiny test request and tells you whether the problem is this device or the API itself, and the Check button re-asks on demand.

entries.title: The heart breaks, then glues itself back together
entries.detail: A connection failure now cracks a heart in two (it beats first, which makes it worse). Below it are the joke, the status strip and two honest choices: try again, or go touch grass - which swaps the screen for a calmer note and a door back. When the API returns, the halves spring together and a green glue seam stitches them up, with a sparkle. The same scene is in Settings under AniList connection, where a check that turns from down to up plays the repair.

entries.title: Every title page can add to Planning
entries.detail: The dashboard's quick-add control is now on the title page wherever it opens - your Library, a studio's filmography, a profile's favourites or activity feed, and the arriving rows. Tap once to put the title on your Planning list; hold the button (or swipe it sideways) to move it straight to Currently Watching. It is the same control, with the same gestures and springs, that the recommendation cards already had.

entries.title: A title already on your list shows its status instead
entries.detail: A show or manga that is already Planned or Watching draws the same badge here as it does on the dashboard, instead of an add button. That is deliberate: AniList's add mutation overwrites the entry, so offering it on a completed title would silently move it back to Planning and lose the status you chose. Titles opened straight from a list carry that status with them, so the badge is right on the first frame.

entries.title: The Activity feed shows a title as soon as you plan it
entries.detail: Planning a title from anywhere used to leave the Activity tab showing the feed as it was before, until the profile was closed and reopened - the feed is loaded once and the tab deliberately does not refetch when you return to it. A list write now refreshes the viewer's own feed, and only their own: somebody else's feed cannot have changed, so it is not refetched.

entries.title: A failed quick add says so on the page
entries.detail: The sheet is opened from four screens and only the dashboard has a snackbar, so a write that failed on the Library or a studio page used to fail silently. The action row now draws the reason under its buttons, and a signed-out reader is told to connect their account rather than being handed a button that does nothing.

entries.title: A title you just planned is not offered again
entries.detail: Planning or editing a title now clears everything a list write made stale, not only the dashboard's own list. Before, a title added from one screen could be served from the detail cache to the next screen with no entry at all, so its page offered to add it a second time, and the profile's totals kept counting the list as it was before the write. The disk copy is dropped with it, so closing and reopening the app cannot bring the old answer back either.

entries.title: The theme is built from the cover's own pixels
entries.detail: Opening a title now reads its cover art and derives the app's colour from the pixels you are looking at, the way Material You reads a wallpaper, instead of trusting AniList's single server-computed average of the whole file. A 128px decode is binned, scored by Material 3's rules - chroma is rewarded, hues are counted as a neighbourhood, and greys are dropped - so a black-and-white cover falls back to AniList's colour and then to the brand blue rather than producing a grey app.

entries.title: Every Material role is now a real tonal palette
entries.detail: The old builder interpolated in HSL, where lightness is not luminance, so contrast and container relationships depended on the seed. A pure-Kotlin HCT/CAM16 engine now builds tonal-spot palettes at Material's fixed tones: 40/80 for primary, 10/90 for containers, 6/98 for surfaces and 30/80 for secondary text. Buttons, chips, the app bar and the sheet all move together because every one of the 36 scheme roles is generated, not just the handful that used to change.

entries.title: The anime theme respects Light, Dark and System
entries.detail: Opening a title used to force the app dark to make the cover theme work, so a light-mode reader was handed a different theme with the show. Both schemes are generated now, and the layer follows the same Theme Mode choice as the rest of the app.

entries.title: Retain Anime Color no longer depends on timing
entries.detail: The sheet read the stored preferences during its first composition, while DataStore was still loading, so a tap that beat the read saw the feature as off and never re-applied it. The colour work now waits for the real settings and then runs once. Retaining writes the anime colour and the standing accent in one transaction, so the app recolours once instead of twice.

entries.title: Colour changes ease instead of cutting
entries.detail: A new scheme cross-fades every role over the same expressive spring the rest of the app uses, and snaps to the end when Motion is set to Instant. Opening a show now reads as the app taking on its colour rather than flashing a second theme.

entries.title: The hero shares the theme's colour
entries.detail: The backdrop, cover shadow and buttons on the title page all read the same extracted seed, so an AniList colour that missed the artwork can no longer make the page and the theme disagree.

entries.title: Startup no longer solves palettes nobody asked for
entries.detail: The generated palettes in the theme picker are built on first read instead of during class initialisation, so a cold start only solves the palette that is actually selected.

entries.title: The title page is the same wherever you open it
entries.detail: Opening a title from your Library, from a studio's filmography or from a profile's favourites gave a sheet with one fewer tab than the same title opened from the dashboard: only the dashboard passed an editor, so the "My Entry" destination was missing and one show was editable from one list and read-only from another. Every host with a session now hands the sheet the same editor, and the entry on that tab is always your own for the media, so the page and its capabilities match wherever the title was opened. A demo or signed-out session is still read-only, and still leaves the tab out rather than drawing one that cannot save.

entries.title: Openings and endings are on the title page
entries.detail: AniList's API carries no theme-song fields at all, so the page now asks AnimeThemes for them and draws an "Openings & Endings" row: each sequence's badge (OP1, ED2) and song title on the title's own banner art, with a count in the heading. The request is made once per title and kept for the day, so re-opening a title or walking a franchise does not spend a second request on songs it already has - this is the one call on the page that does not come out of AniList's budget, and the service behind it is volunteer-run and rate-limited. A title AnimeThemes has nothing for simply leaves the row out, and the play control hands the clip to whatever you already watch video with rather than shipping a video player for six-second sequences.

entries.title: Genres and tags are one Categories section
entries.detail: The two separate Genres and Tags cards are now one block under one heading: the genres first, then AniList's weighted tags with their match percentages, so "Kaiju 93%" sits next to the genres it belongs with. The tag list opens on the strongest few with a "more" control that is remembered per title, instead of twenty chips covering a third of the screen before the synopsis. Tags AniList marks as spoilers are no longer dropped either - they were left out of the chips while the heading still counted them, and they now sit behind their own strip that reveals nothing until you ask.

entries.title: Every other AniList link is listed
entries.detail: AniList files more for a title than where it streams - the official site, news, a soundtrack page - and only the streaming entries were drawn. Those keep their own "Where to Watch" card, and everything else now has an "External Links" section under the details, so Crunchyroll no longer appears twice while the official site did not appear at all. A link with no name or no URL is dropped rather than drawn as a chip that opens nothing, and duplicates collapse to one.

entries.title: Titles, synonyms and producers get their own rows
entries.detail: Alternative titles were a card of label/value pairs, synonyms were poured into one of those pairs, and the publishers were mixed into the specs grid's studio row. Each is now a disclosure row - Titles, Synonyms, Producers - and tapping one opens a sheet with the complete list, which is what keeps six producers and fifteen synonyms from doubling the page's length while keeping them one tap away. Producers are the credits AniList does not mark as the main studio, so a payload with no such credit simply leaves the row out.

entries.title: The score slider follows the account's score format
entries.detail: The entry editor worked out its slider's scale from the loaded number - anything above ten meant a hundred-point account - so a hundred-point entry scored 8 or 10 opened on a 0-10 slider and could not be moved to the score the reader wanted, and five- and three-point accounts were offered values AniList rejects. The entry load now asks for `Viewer.mediaListOptions.scoreFormat` in the same request and the slider's ceiling comes from the account.

entries.title: Half-point scores are reachable from the slider
entries.detail: Every scale got one tick per whole point, so a decimal account whose row already read 8.5 / 10 could only drag the thumb to 8 or 9. Ticks now follow the format's own step - a tenth on `POINT_10_DECIMAL`, a whole point on the integer formats - and each drag is snapped to a value that format actually holds. A score loaded from AniList is left alone until the slider is touched, so opening the form never rewrites it.

entries.title: Three small controls now meet the 48dp touch target
entries.detail: The progress stepper's plus and minus buttons were 42dp, the composer's formatting buttons 40dp, and a comment's options button 36dp - all below Android's minimum touch target. Only the boxes around the glyphs grew; the icons inside are the size they were.

entries.title: Relations can tell a source from its adaptation
entries.detail: The relation query asked for `relationType` at version 1, whose enum has no `SOURCE`, so a light novel and the anime made from it both arrived as `ADAPTATION` and the row could not say which was which. Both the list and detail queries now ask for version 2, so the adapter finally receives the value its existing "Source" label was written for.

entries.title: The filter bar's clear button is a full-size target
entries.detail: The control that undoes a filter was sized to its 28dp glyph, making it the smallest target on a bar full of chips. The glyph is still 28dp; the area a finger has to hit is now 48dp.

entries.title: Clearing an edit date no longer opens the picker
entries.detail: The X beside a date was a 20dp icon inside a row that was itself clickable, so a near miss opened the date picker instead of clearing the date. The X now has its own 48dp hit area and consumes the tap before the picker sees it.

entries.title: Long pages can be navigated by heading
entries.detail: TalkBack could only read the title page, profile tabs and settings as one long list. Section titles, settings card titles and profile section headers now carry heading semantics, so they appear in the screen reader's heading navigation.

entries.title: Settings states the app's privacy position
entries.detail: The About card now says plainly that AniSequel talks only to AniList and GitHub Releases, with no analytics, no telemetry and no third-party tracker.

entries.title: Private notes can be written and cleared
entries.detail: The entry editor now loads, edits and saves AniList's private `notes` field, which the app was already reading but never showed. An empty field is sent as an explicit clear; saves from callers that do not edit notes omit the argument so they cannot erase a note they never loaded.

entries.title: Charts can be read aloud
entries.detail: The status and format strips now expose one spoken summary of the shares they draw, and each bar or format row reads as a single phrase - label, count and percentage - instead of unrelated numbers.

entries.title: Where to Watch lists the streaming services
entries.detail: The title page now asks for AniList's `externalLinks` and draws the services that carry the show above the synopsis. Only `STREAMING` links with a name and a URL are shown, duplicate regional entries collapse to one chip, and each 48dp chip opens the service in the browser.

entries.title: A long bio cannot blank every cover
entries.detail: Cover links were aliased into one GraphQL document, so an over-complex bio could be refused whole and leave every poster on a placeholder with nothing on screen to explain it. Links are now requested ten at a time; a refused batch costs only its own cards, the successful batches are kept, and the refusal is logged instead of disappearing.

entries.title: Creator pages show their works again
entries.detail: The staff profile asked AniList for `staffMedia` but declared the field as `media`, so Moshi never filled it and every creator's work row was empty while the same row on a character page rendered normally. The response is now mapped to the right field. The row also asks for twenty-five credits instead of twelve and collapses the several edges one title can occupy - a director who also wrote and storyboarded a film - so twelve edges can no longer turn into four posters. When one title arrives with several roles, the person's primary occupation wins over whichever credit AniList happened to list first.

entries.title: Works come before the biography
entries.detail: A long biography was measured first and pushed the row the page exists for below the sheet's viewport, which read as the works never having loaded. The appearance and voiced-character rows now sit above the biography, and a creator's heading reads "Worked on" rather than "Appears in".

entries.title: Music videos appear on their shows again
entries.detail: AniList attaches a music video through a CHARACTER relation, the same type it uses for crossovers, so the relation row removed every song from every show that had one. A CHARACTER edge is now kept when either end is a music video, labelled "Music video", and ranked ahead of a long franchise's specials so the cap does not hide it.

entries.title: Manga relations carry their length
entries.detail: Relation cards read only `episodes`, so a manga card showed its format and year but silently dropped its length. Cards now read chapters, or volumes when the chapter count is unknown, and a manga page's section heading is "Volumes & Relations" instead of "Seasons & Relations".

entries.title: Relations cannot mix up an anime and a manga
entries.detail: The relation row deduplicated by numeric id, and the detail map the screens read was keyed the same way, so a manga sharing a number with an anime could show the anime's poster, synopsis and cast. Both now compare the media namespace as well as the id, and a detail fetched for one namespace is never drawn for the other.

entries.title: The full-screen cover fits the artwork
entries.detail: The viewer drew every cover into a fixed 340x440 window, which letterboxed a 2:3 poster on one axis, and its pan limits were the constants 300 and 400 regardless of screen or image size. The frame is now the largest box that fits the image's own aspect ratio, and the pan bounds are measured from the drawn cover.

entries.title: Covers start loading sooner
entries.detail: The image client inherited OkHttp's default of five requests per host, so a relation row or a library grid downloaded five covers while the rest waited. The image dispatcher now allows sixteen per host, keeps a matching connection pool warm across a scroll, and still leaves the rate-limited GraphQL client untouched.

entries.title: The parent's cover keeps its shape
entries.detail: The prequel/parent card cropped its cover into a 48dp square, cutting the faces off the top and the title off the bottom of a 2:3 poster. It is now a 48dp-wide poster at the app's cover ratio, centred against the text.

entries.title: The Airing filter now shows airing sequels
entries.detail: Choosing Airing in the filter compared the card's display label, 'Airing', with AniList's raw status, 'RELEASING', so the filter always came back empty even when the dashboard was showing releasing shows. It now uses the same predicate as the status chip, so the filter and the card agree.

entries.title: The release-year chart is chronological again
entries.detail: The Stats tab re-sorted year buckets by their printed labels, which put '19 before 1995 because an apostrophe sorts before a digit and pushed every pre-2000 year to the end of the chart. The buckets are already tallied and ordered by real year, so they now keep that order.

entries.title: A progress or score revert is no longer lost mid-save
entries.detail: If you changed a value, then changed it back while the first request was still on the wire, the coalescer dropped the revert because it still believed the server held the original value. The revert is now queued as a compensating write, and closing an editor waits for a request that is already in flight instead of returning immediately.

entries.title: The app lock swallows taps and survives rotation
entries.detail: The lock screen hid the list but did not consume pointer input, so taps and drags could still reach the live screen underneath. Every event is now consumed except the Unlock button's. Rotating the phone no longer re-arms the lock after you have unlocked it, and a biometric prompt that cannot be shown no longer leaves the Unlock button permanently inert.

entries.title: An OAuth callback is handled once
entries.detail: The callback Intent stays attached to the Activity, so rotating the phone replayed the same redirect and re-saved the token (or re-showed a cancelled sign-in error). It is now handled only when the Activity is first created; callbacks that arrive while the app is already open still go through onNewIntent.

entries.title: One auth session for the whole process
entries.detail: The auth repository was rebuilt on every rotation while the retained ViewModel kept the old one, leaving two token caches and defeating the network client's cache. It now lives in the Application, so the Activity and its ViewModel always share one session. Keystore encryption and token decryption have also moved off the main thread.

entries.title: A custom canvas colour is a dark-mode choice again
entries.detail: The canvas choices are all dark colours and the setting is described as a dark-mode preference, but the colour was also applied in light mode, where it left dark text on a nearly black background. It now applies only to the dark theme, so switching to light mode restores readable contrast.

entries.title: Selection is announced, not just coloured
entries.detail: Filter chips and segmented controls showed their selected state only through colour. They now expose selected state and the right control role to accessibility services, so a screen reader can say which filter or tab is active.

entries.title: Retained anime colours stay retained
entries.detail: Retain Anime Color could still lose the colour. Closing a sheet with the revert timer on Immediately switched the anime layer off even though Retain was on, and turning Retain off again did not return you to your previous theme because the layer outranks every other colour source. The layer now outlives the sheet whenever the colour is being retained, switching Retain off actually ends it, and disabling the anime layer always clears the cover colour instead of leaving a stale one to reappear. The temporary 5- and 10-minute choices also work now: their timer used to be cancelled the moment the sheet closed, so a temporary colour behaved exactly like a retained one.

entries.title: Update checks use the repository's current address
entries.detail: The in-app updater, the Settings privacy note and the README still named the account the project used before it was renamed. GitHub redirects the old address today, but a redirect is not a contract; every link now uses the current repository name so update checks keep reaching the release assets directly.

entries.title: Comments now have a real editor, with formatting and a preview
entries.detail: The comment box was a two-line strip at the bottom of a long thread. It is now a full editor opened from the bar under the thread: Cancel keeps your draft, Write/Preview renders the comment exactly as the markdown parser will draw it, and the format bar wraps the selected text in bold, italic or spoiler markers. Tapping Reply on a comment starts the draft with that person's @name already in it, the counter shows how much of AniList's 8,000 characters is used, and a disabled Post button now says why instead of refusing on send. Images can be attached by URL, because AniList has no upload endpoint.

entries.title: A repeated comment id can no longer crash a thread
entries.detail: The comment list is keyed by comment id, and Compose treats two rows with the same key as a fatal error - the thread crashed while drawing instead of showing the comment. The list has two sources, the fetch and the comment a post returns, and they are now collapsed to one entry per id: the posted copy replaces the fetched one, and the scroll to a new comment looks the comment up by id rather than assuming its position.

entries.title: Your AniList token is encrypted on the device now
entries.detail: The token that lets AniSequel read and write your AniList account used to sit in plain text inside the app's private storage. It is now encrypted with a key that never leaves the Android keystore, and an existing session is migrated the first time this version opens. If the device's screen lock is removed and the key is invalidated, AniSequel asks you to sign in again instead of failing on every launch. Nothing about signing in or staying signed in otherwise changes.

entries.title: An optional app lock keeps your list private
entries.detail: Settings > Edit now has a Privacy card with a Lock AniSequel switch. When it is on, opening the app or coming back from the background asks for your fingerprint, face or screen lock before your list appears, and the recents preview is blanked while it is locked. It is off by default, and it is unavailable on a device with no screen lock because there would be nothing to ask for. Back from the lock screen sends the app to the background rather than dismissing the lock.

entries.title: A throttled empty answer can no longer wipe your list
entries.detail: AniList sometimes answers a list request with a well-formed collection that has no entries - under load, or while rate limiting. AniSequel used to store that answer, so a temporary failure looked exactly like an account that had deleted everything. An empty response is now refused when the app already holds a populated list for the same account; the list you were reading stays, and the failed refresh says so.

entries.title: Title pages cache by release status, and a passed episode overrides the cache
entries.detail: Every title's synopsis, cast and studios were kept for the same flat day. A finished show now stays cached for a week because its facts are settled; a currently airing show is refreshed after three hours, and an announced-but-unreleased one after six. Separately, if the cached next episode's airing time has already passed, the record is treated as out of date immediately rather than waiting for its window - the countdown on screen can no longer describe an episode that has already aired.

entries.title: A pull-to-refresh is no longer treated like a background check
entries.detail: Two refreshes now have two cooldowns: a deliberate pull or button press may run again after five seconds, while an automatic check on returning to the app waits fifteen. The five-second floor still absorbs the accidental double pull, and the automatic one stops a resume moments after a failed refresh from spending another request to learn the same thing.

entries.title: A malformed image size in a bio can no longer crash the page
entries.detail: AniList's image syntax carries a size, and a malformed or hostile one - an image billions of pixels wide - overflowed the layout and took the screen down with it. Width and height are now clamped to generous ceilings, so real artwork is untouched and an absurd number draws at the page's width instead. Parsed bios and comments are also cached for the process now, so scrolling one out of view and back no longer re-tokenizes the whole document or replays its height animation.

entries.title: Widgets decode covers inside a memory budget
entries.detail: Each widget cover now gets a slice of a budget computed from the display and divided by the number of images the update decodes, instead of a fixed pixel ceiling that was the same on every device. A refresh whose cover is already in memory answers immediately rather than queueing behind another download, and every bitmap handed to the launcher is a software bitmap - a hardware bitmap cannot cross into the home screen's process, which is why a tile could come out blank on some devices with no other symptom.

entries.title: A huge error response can no longer exhaust memory
entries.detail: When AniList refused a request, the app read the entire response body to find the reason - even when the body was not AniList's small error envelope but a proxy's page or a hostile response. That read is now capped at 64 KB. The HTTP status still classifies the failure exactly as before; the body was never trusted for anything else.

entries.title: The app has a bar of its own now: Home, Library, and your profile
entries.detail: Everything the app does that is about you rather than about one title now lives on a page you can reach from one place. A floating capsule sits at the bottom of the main pages with three stops - Home, your Library, and your profile, drawn as your own AniList avatar. Switching between them springs rather than cuts: the selected tab grows the name of the page it belongs to, exactly as the title sheet's own capsule does, because it is the same control. Back from any of the three lands on Home instead of walking back through every tab visited, a repeat tap on the tab you are already on does nothing, and returning to a page restores what it was showing. The bar draws itself only over those pages: a screen opened from one of them - Settings, the tier list, a studio, somebody else's profile - keeps the whole screen.

entries.title: The Library is your own page now, not a tab of every profile
entries.detail: The list was the fourth tab of every profile, including a stranger's, which made the thing you consult most often one tap deeper than the thing you consult least - and it spent a tab of every profile on the one list that profile was least likely to be opened for. It is now the app's second page: your own anime and manga as posters, with the same type, filter, sort and search as before, and the same memory - the view you left it on and the place in it are still there when you come back. The profile kept what a profile is for: the person, their activity, their numbers, and their social graph. A profile no longer draws the Library chip at all, and every profile is four tabs instead of five.

entries.title: A profile's own pages sit under its top bar
entries.detail: With the app's bar at the bottom edge, the profile could not keep a second capsule against the same edge - two bars stacked is two answers to one question. Home, Activity, Stats and Social now switch from directly under the profile's top bar, where they read as the sections of one page rather than as places to go. And the two ways into your own profile agree: the avatar in the dashboard's top bar, the avatar on the Library page, and the face on the bar are one tap to one screen.

entries.title: Opening a tab and scrolling it in one motion no longer takes the app down
entries.detail: The container that switches between the detail sheet's page and its editor - and the one that switches the Settings tabs - animated its own height while the tab underneath it was still arriving, so the scrollable page was measured again on every frame of the switch, against a height that had not settled yet. The height now snaps to the tab being shown and only the fade and the slide play, so a reader who scrolls while a tab is arriving is measured once, against a height that is already final. The markdown table reader also refuses a start index before the start of its own document rather than reading off the front of the line list.

entries.title: A character or staff page opens with a cover, the way a studio's does
entries.detail: Opening a character or a staff member gave a plain heading and a list, while a studio's page had the art behind it, the facts in one header, and a clear hierarchy. A person's page now opens the same way: the portrait on a cover-style header, with the name, the native name, the favourites count and the rest of the facts AniList sends - for a character and for a person who made the work alike.

entries.title: A character's page says who voiced them
entries.detail: The thing a character's page is asked most often - who plays them - was the one thing missing, even though AniList sends it with the character's own record. The page now carries a Voiced by section: the languages the character was played in, the actors' faces and names beside them, and every row opens that actor's own page.

entries.title: A person's page lists the titles they worked on, and the characters they played
entries.detail: A staff member's page ended at a name and a picture. It now lists the titles the record carries - AniList's own role label and the year beside each poster - and, below them, the characters that person voiced, so an actor's page can be walked back to the work. Every row opens the title or the character the same way any other card does.

entries.title: Reopening a person no longer buys them a second time
entries.detail: Every look at a character or a staff member re-fetched the whole record, so closing the sheet and tapping the same face again was a fresh round trip for an answer already in hand. The fetched person is now remembered for the session: a re-open draws the page from memory, and only a person never fetched is asked for.

entries.title: Favourites are split into characters and staff
entries.detail: AniList's favourites were fused into a single run of faces in which a voice actor and a character could sit side by side. The profile now lists Favourite Characters and Favourite Staff as their own sections, each in the API's order, so the two kinds of favourite can be read for what they are.

entries.title: The Library comes back the way you left it
entries.detail: The Library always reopened at its defaults, whatever had been chosen before. The type, the filter, the sort and its direction are now remembered and restored together, so leaving the Library and coming back - or reopening the app - returns the list that was being read.

entries.title: Images in a synopsis now draw
entries.detail: AniList's synopses are markdown, and their images - a GIF pasted as a URL, or an HTML img tag - were printed as text or dropped outright. Both now render as images, protocol-relative addresses resolve to HTTPS, and HTML entities in the text decode instead of arriving as ampersand codes.

entries.title: The relations row reads as a franchise, in story order
entries.detail: The row of other entries was wrong in both directions before it was right: keeping only anime emptied a manga page of its own volumes, and keeping only the subject's own medium then hid the adaptation - AniList files an adaptation on both sides, so a Cowboy Bebop manga could no longer see the anime, and the anime could not see the manga. The row now carries the same-medium entries plus the cross-medium adaptation, and it is ordered rather than left in the order the API happened to insert it: the prequels, sequels and parent first, oldest first, the adaptation next, the side stories and spin-offs after them - so the entry a reader came for is inside the row's cap on a franchise with fifty relations.

entries.title: An empty answer is shown as empty, not as a load that never ends
entries.detail: A response that came back with nothing - an empty list, a null block from the API - was read as still waiting on some pages: a spinner where an empty state belongs, or a count still pretending. Empty answers now reach the screen as they are - the empty state, a zero where a count lives, and no second request pretending the answer never arrived.

entries.title: Being rate-limited now says so
entries.detail: AniList answers a burst of requests with a refusal, and the app turned that refusal into a generic failure or into nothing at all. A rate-limited answer now raises one notice at the top of the screen - AniList is busy, give it a minute and try again - instead of leaving a page quietly empty or an error that blames the request.

entries.title: A relation opens the whole page, not a slice of it
entries.detail: Tapping a related title inside a page opened a visibly emptier page than the same title opened from the list: "no synopsis available", no credits, no studios, and the relations row gone after a single hop. The sheet did fetch the full record - the page was handed the thin relation node the card carried, so the answer was thrown away. A relation now resolves through the fetched detail exactly the way an arriving row already did, and keeps the progress from the entry you tapped.

entries.title: The progress wave stops redrawing the page it sits on
entries.detail: The wavy progress bar read its animation state during composition, so every frame of the wave recomposed the page around it, and its fill started from zero again whenever the row came back into view or you followed a relation to another title. The wave is drawn in the draw phase now, a bar with nothing to show composes no animation at all, and the fill slides to the new value across a hop instead of replaying its entrance.

entries.title: Your list is still there when you reopen the app
entries.detail: The list, your own profile and every title page were held in memory only, so closing the app threw all of it away and the next launch bought the whole list back from AniList - a request per chunk of it - before it could draw a single row. All of it is now snapshotted under the cache directory, so a launch inside its window spends nothing. Signing out deletes all of it.

entries.title: A title's synopsis, cast and studios are remembered for a day
entries.detail: Opening a title re-fetched its whole record on every launch, even one already read through a minute earlier. That record - synopsis, cast, staff, studios, release year, relations - is now reused for 24 hours, so the page opens full and instantly; what genuinely moves inside it, like the score or the next airing episode, is asked for again the next day.

entries.title: Your own profile is re-fetched at most every half hour
entries.detail: Every launch began with a request no screen had asked for: the viewer's own profile, needed before the dashboard could name the account or ask for a list. It is now reused for thirty minutes. A pasted token is still checked against AniList first - the caches are cleared before that check, so a stored profile can never vouch for a session AniList has refused.

entries.title: Your own comments can now be edited or deleted
entries.detail: A comment could be written and liked, and that was the end of it: a typo was permanent and a comment you no longer stood behind stayed in somebody else's thread. Your own comments now carry an options menu that leads to an editor - seeded with the text on screen - and to a delete behind a confirmation. Both go through AniList, so the thread everyone reads is the one you changed, and a delete moves the activity's comment count with it. Only your own comments get the menu; drawing it on anybody else's would be inviting a tap the server refuses.

entries.title: The comment box enforces AniList's own limits
entries.detail: AniList refuses a comment shorter than two characters, and the sheet used to send it anyway and print the server's refusal as a failure - a lone letter or emoji was a round trip that could only end badly. The send button now waits for a second character and says why, the field stops accepting text at the eight thousand the schema allows rather than letting you write a comment that will bounce, and the keyboard's Send action posts exactly the way the button does.

entries.title: Waiting screens are drawn as the screen that is coming
entries.detail: The activity feed, a comment thread, the likers sheet and the Social tab answered every load with a spinner in the middle of an otherwise empty page, then replaced it with the full layout. Each now draws a shimmering sketch of the rows it is about to show - the card, the comment, the face - at the sizes those rows actually have, so the data lands into a layout you were already looking at instead of replacing one.

entries.title: A failed likers list offers a way back
entries.detail: The sheet that answers who liked an activity printed its failure as a sentence with no way forward, unlike the comment thread, whose failure offers the request one tap away. The same failure now carries the same Try again button.

entries.title: Very large lists no longer come back quietly short
entries.detail: An account whose list spans more than ten of AniList's chunks was cut off at the tenth, and the shortened list was cached as if it had arrived complete - so sequels near the end of the list never appeared and reloading never changed it. The list now follows AniList's own paging to the end, and in the one case it cannot - more chunks than a single load will chase - it says so instead of keeping a short list.

entries.title: Opening hundreds of titles no longer keeps all of them in memory
entries.detail: The synopsis, cast and studios a card fetches when you open it were capped in one cache but kept alive by a second, unbounded one, so a long session held every title it had ever opened. Both caches now share the same bound, and the title on screen is the last one that bound would drop.

entries.title: The rolling stat counters keep a steady width
entries.detail: The number that rolls when your stats change was drawn with proportional digits, so the text measured differently for every count it passed through - "111" is narrower than "888" - and the row it sits in was re-measured on every frame of the animation. The digits are fixed-width now, so the roll costs what settled text costs and nothing beside it jumps.

entries.title: A character's page lists their manga, not only their anime
entries.detail: The titles under a character were filtered to anime, so a character's page omitted the source manga of the very show it was opened from - and the format line under every poster exists precisely because an appearance can be either medium. An actor's page never filtered, so a voice actor listed manga credits their character's page hid. Both kinds now draw the same list, with each poster saying which medium it is.

entries.title: A long biography no longer buries the rest of a person's page
entries.detail: A person's sheet caps its height so the portrait and the name stay on screen when it opens, but the cap was a crop rather than a viewport: a long biography measured first and took all the remaining height, leaving the titles that person appears in - and the Open on AniList link - measured into zero and impossible to reach. The sheet scrolls now, so it still opens on the face and everything under it is one swipe away.

entries.title: Years active read as one span, not two loose years
entries.detail: AniList records a staff member's active years as a start and end pair, with a single year meaning they are still working. The sheet joined the pair with a comma, so a career running 1963 to 2013 printed as Active 1963, 2013 - two years with a fifty-year hole between them. The span now prints as the one it is, and a working career as since 1998.

entries.title: A studio's header facts wrap instead of running off the screen
entries.detail: A studio header draws up to three capsules - what kind of company it is, how many favourites it has, and how many titles it worked on - in a row that could not wrap. Together they are wider than a small phone's margin, so on the studios popular enough to have all three, the title count was clipped off the right edge where it could not be read. The header wraps the capsules now: nothing changes on a wide screen, and a narrow one stops hiding a fact.

entries.title: Inline spoilers open where they sit
entries.detail: `~!...!~` inside a sentence was drawn as a covered run with no way to reach the text: tapping it did nothing, while the same token on a line of its own had a chip that revealed fine - so a plot point written mid-paragraph stayed covered for good. The covered run is the tap target now, two spoilers in one paragraph open independently of each other, and a reveal survives scrolling away from the paragraph and back.

entries.title: Picking a palette or a hue changes the app again
entries.detail: With Dynamic colour on, tapping a palette or a hue lit the card and moved the check mark while the wallpaper scheme kept drawing: the wallpaper outranks both in the theme, and nothing stepped it off. A palette or hue pick now switches the wallpaper off, turning Dynamic colour on steps the anime colour layer off, and the card's caption names the source actually driving the app instead of naming a colour that is being overruled.

entries.title: The artwork no longer changes under your eyes as a title opens
entries.detail: A sheet opened from the dashboard drew the poster first and swapped to the banner the moment the detail response landed - a second full-size image fetched, decoded and drawn in the middle of the entrance animation. The hero is the key visual again, the way it was designed to be, so the artwork on the first frame is the artwork you keep.

entries.title: Covers draw at the size they are shown at
entries.detail: A person's appearance row asked AniList for the 230px cover and drew it at 112dp - about 336px on a 3x screen - so every poster under a character or a staff member was upscaled, and titles opened from those rows kept the smaller cover even after the detail response had handed over the larger one. Both now use the bigger size.

entries.title: Opening a title does less work on the frame you tap
entries.detail: The page rebuilt its tag list, cast, relations and alternative titles on every recomposition while the sheet animated in, and the anime colour layer re-themed the whole app in two separate waves - one for the anime colour, one for the retained accent. The derived lists are computed once per title and the colour layer lands in a single write, so the entrance has the frames to itself.

entries.title: Save and Delete are always within reach on the Edit tab
entries.detail: They were the last row of a form taller than the sheet on a small screen, so the button that keeps an edit sat below the fold. The two actions are pinned under the fields now, and they say what state they are in: the bar reads "No changes to save yet" until the draft differs from what AniList holds, Save sends nothing until then, and a save's confirmation no longer stays up after the next change.

entries.title: Motion style reaches the app the moment you choose it
entries.detail: The Motion style setting was written to a value that composition could not observe, so most of the app kept the springs it had been composed with - the dashboard went on overshooting on Smooth, and Instant only sped up whatever happened to rebuild next. The tokens are observable state now, and the navigation bar's selected item springs open to its width instead of jumping to it.

entries.title: Links with parentheses in them no longer break
entries.detail: A link to a Wikipedia article - the shape AniList bios use most - cut itself at the first bracket. `Spike_Spiegel_(Cowboy_Bebop)` linked to `Spike_Spiegel_(Cowboy_Bebop`, which is a page that does not exist, and the closing bracket was left sitting in the sentence as stray text. The same happened to a bare URL between two words. Both now keep the whole address, while a bracket that closes the link rather than the URL still stays out of it, so a sentence keeps its own punctuation.

entries.title: A cover you can tap takes you to the title
entries.detail: A cover image wrapped in a link - the way a bio points at the show a character is from - took you to the artwork instead of the show. The pattern that reads that shape existed but was never given to the parser, so the ordinary link rule read the cover as the target and dropped the title entirely. Tapping the cover now opens the title, with the cover still drawn inside it.

entries.title: Spoilers open again
entries.detail: The chip that reveals a spoiler stopped responding, so nothing behind it would ever show. The cause was subtle: the chip asked the app's press animation to work without telling it where the press was coming from, so the animation installed its own second gesture handler to guess - and two handlers competing for one tap meant the tap never arrived. Every other press control in the app already shares one signal between the two; this one now does too. The chip also wraps to its label instead of stretching the length of the card.

entries.title: The anime theme now overrides the whole palette, not a quarter of it
entries.detail: The anime theme set the accent and left the rest of Material's palette exactly where it found it, so a Chainsaw Man page had a red button over purple borders and purple secondary text - the roles the theme never overrode were not unstyled, they were Material's default purple. The theme is now built on the app's own colour set rather than Material's baseline, so every surface, border and container in the app follows the title you opened. The status colours and the secondary text colour are deliberately left alone: they were hand-picked for contrast, and tinting text toward a show's colour is how labels stop being readable.

entries.title: Characters and the people who made them open inside the app
entries.detail: Tapping a face in the cast handed you to your browser - the one thing on a title page that did, when a studio credit opens a studio page without leaving the app. A character now opens their own page here instead: their picture, the other names they are known by, their age and gender, their birth date and blood type where AniList has them, how many people have them in their favourites, their biography rendered the same way a bio is, and the titles they appear in as covers you can tap. The crew row does the same for whoever made it - a director gets their roles, the years they were active and where they are from, which is information a credit never carried. Both work from everywhere a title can be opened - a title on the dashboard, a title on someone's profile, a title on a studio's page - and tapping a title from a person's page takes you to that title in turn, so you can walk from an actor to their next credit without going back out. Both sheets read what AniList offers and stop short: the comment thread and the edit history are still one tap away on AniList itself.

entries.title: A cast card you can read is a cast card you can open
entries.detail: Nothing to tap, and nothing to notice: on the dashboard and on a studio's page, a face in the cast and a name in the crew were captions, while the same rows on someone's profile opened a full page. Both now open, and both say so in the same way. The one place they deliberately still do not is the offline demo, which has no cast to look anyone up in - there they stay captions rather than becoming buttons that could only report a failure.

entries.title: The synopsis and the studios are back
entries.detail: Opening a title could show no synopsis, no studio and sometimes no cast or crew at all. The page's request to AniList had picked up one stray argument - it asked the studios list for a page size, which is not something that list has - and AniList checks a whole request before answering any of it, so the mistake cost the entire response rather than the studios alone. Everything the title page cannot show without came back empty together: the synopsis, every studio credit and the studio in the artwork header, the characters and voice actors, the staff, the tags, the rankings and the trailer. The dashboard hid most of it because it merges the answer into the list entry it already had, which is why this looked like two separate faults instead of one.

entries.title: One way out of a title page, not two
entries.detail: Tapping a related title used to open it with a second copy of the close button and a second Open on AniList button sitting on top of its own. The page keeps its scroll position per title so a new one starts at the top, but the bar that appears once you scroll past the artwork was holding on to the title you had just left, and it never stood down. The bar is now built from the title actually on screen, so it arrives when you scroll and gets out of the way when you do not.

entries.title: A manga's page lists manga
entries.detail: The related titles on a title page were filtered to anime no matter what you had open. On an anime that is right - it is what keeps a show's light novel and guidebook out of the row next to its sequels - but on a manga it was exactly backwards: One Piece's fifty-one relations are almost all manga, a spin-off per volume, a side story, a prequel, and the anime ones are all adaptations. So opening a manga showed you a shelf of TV episodes and none of the manga's own franchise. The row now lists the same medium as the title you are reading, which fixes the manga side and leaves the anime side exactly as it was, because AniList files an adaptation in both directions.

entries.title: The synopsis stops printing its own credit line
entries.detail: AniList ends a description with a provenance line - One Piece's with (Source: VIZ Media), most with (Source: AniList) or (Source: Wikipedia). The title page renders descriptions through AniList's own markdown, so that line was being read as a paragraph and printed in body type under the last line of the story, where it reads as part of the synopsis. It also counted toward the length test that decides whether to offer Read more, so a description that comfortably fitted on screen grew a button anyway. The credit is removed, along with every one of them on a long description rather than only the last.

entries.title: Pinned studios open
entries.detail: Every other favourites row on a profile went somewhere - anime and manga open the title page, characters and staff hand off to the browser - and the studios were the only row that did nothing at all. They looked like controls, which is worse than looking like text. A studio somebody has pinned is the strongest thing on the profile about the kind of thing they watch, and the studio's own page was already built and already used by the credits on a title page, so this was a dead end pointed at a door that already existed. Each chip now opens that studio, and says whether it animates or publishes - a distinction the studio page leads with and a name alone does not carry.

entries.title: The anime theme reaches the background
entries.detail: The anime theme changed the accent and left everything else exactly where it was, so a Chainsaw Man page and a Frieren page had the same navy backdrop with a differently-coloured button on it. The setting is for feeling like the show you opened, and the background and the surfaces the cards sit on are the part a reader actually looks at - so the surface ladder now takes the show's colour, at a saturation low enough that it tints rather than repaints. Lightness is untouched, which is what keeps the text exactly as legible as it was. A custom accent chosen in Settings still moves the accent only: that is a standing preference, and the background there moves on purpose or not at all.

entries.title: Comments can be liked
entries.detail: A comment could be read and never liked. AniList lists comments as likeable in its own right - a different kind from an activity, and a separate set of ids - and the app was already fetching each comment's liked state and throwing it away: the data was there, paid for on every thread, and nothing ever drew a heart. Each comment now has one, in the same place and the same style as the one under the activity it belongs to, and a signed-out reader gets a disabled heart rather than one that looks live and does nothing.

entries.title: The comment sheet survives a tab switch
entries.detail: Opening a thread and then tapping another tab took the whole sheet down with it - mid-sentence, half-typed comment and all. The sheet was drawn by the tab, and the tab is thrown away when the switch finishes; the sheet lives in its own window, so it went with the tab. The list of people who liked an activity had already been moved out for this exact reason and carried a note saying why, and the comment sheet had been left behind, which left the two on the same screen behaving differently for no reason either could explain. Both are now drawn by the profile itself.

entries.title: Everything in its own folder, and each folder says what belongs in it
entries.detail: Three screens had their main file sitting loose while their own parts lived in a subdirectory, unlike every other screen in the app. Each of those four layers now carries a short README saying what belongs there, what the rule for placing a file is, and which mistake has already been made in it - so the next person knows where a file goes without reading the whole tree first. The rule of thumb is one question: would this file move if the screen it belongs to moved?

entries.title: The whole cast, and everything AniList knows about them
entries.detail: The cast row stopped at twelve and asked AniList for three things: a name, a portrait and who plays them - which is what a poster already tells you. It now asks for the full twenty-five and for what the API actually knows: the character's other names, their age and gender, and how many people have them in their favourites. So Spike Spiegel is no longer just Spike Spiegel - he is also Spike Spike and Swimming Bird, twenty-seven, fourteen thousand people' favourite - and a supporting character with four thousand likes is visibly a different proposition from one with nine. Each character opens their AniList page, where the rest of it lives, the same way a studio credit opens that studio's filmography rather than drawing it.

entries.title: Spoilers hide behind a chip you can see
entries.detail: The control that reveals a spoiler was a line of text inside the block, set close enough to the body text beneath it that scanning a bio could not tell where the hidden part began - which is the one thing a spoiler has to say before it is opened. It is now a pill sitting on the block's top edge, the only thing visible while the spoiler is closed, with an eye and a label that says whether tapping will show or hide. Reading a revealed spoiler no longer risks closing it: the text takes no taps, so a thumb resting on the card cannot hide what you were reading and a link inside the spoiler can be opened.

entries.title: A link that cannot open now hands you the link
entries.detail: Tapping a link in somebody's bio could do nothing at all - no browser, no error, no hint. The app opened links inside a guard that threw failures away, so a phone without the app for a steam or Spotify link, or a bare anilist.co slug, just sat there. Those are ordinary links in an ordinary bio rather than an edge case. A link that cannot be opened is now put on your clipboard with a line saying so, so you can paste it into a browser or send it to yourself. Links the app vouched for - the ones on a title page - still just open, and a failure there stays quiet.

entries.title: Studios open: every credit is now a page you can follow
entries.detail: A studio name on a title page used to be text and nothing else. Every credit is now a chip, and tapping one opens that studio - its name, whether it animates or publishes, how many people have favourited it, and everything AniList credits it with, shelved by year so a filmography reads as a history instead of one endless column. Announced work gets its own shelf at the top, where a title with no date would otherwise be sorted to the bottom. Tap a poster to open that title, hold it to see the artwork on its own.

entries.title: Every studio on a title, not only the main one
entries.detail: The title page asked AniList for its main studios only, so the publishers, licensors and producers filed in the same connection were never fetched - and the names it did show were printed as one comma-joined line. AniList answers studios with both a flat list and an edges list that says which credit is the title's own, so the page now asks for both, draws every credit as a chip, and fills the ones that actually made the show. A name with no id is still shown, because it is still part of the answer to who made this - it just cannot be followed.

entries.title: Spoilers reveal and hide on a button instead of any tap
entries.detail: A revealed spoiler closed again on any tap at all, which made the block unusable while reading: a thumb resting on the card hid the text, and a link inside a spoiler could not be opened because the tap that reached it was swallowed by the toggle. The reveal is its own control now, the text underneath behaves like any other paragraph, and an explicit Hide closes it - which is also the only thing on screen that says a spoiler can be closed.

entries.title: The progress wave is one wave again
entries.detail: The coloured part of Watching Progress was drawn as its own wave, with its own height and its own moving phase, so it floated above the track it was supposed to be the beginning of - a short squiggle over a longer one, with its round head off the curve entirely. The fill is now the same path as the track, clipped to the watched part, so the two cannot drift apart: one curve, the first stretch of it coloured in.

entries.title: Titles opened from a profile no longer say Unknown Title
entries.detail: Opening a title from an Activity row showed a page titled Unknown Title with the right studio, status, synopsis and cast underneath it. The title page's request never asked AniList for a title, which went unnoticed on the dashboard because that path merges the response into the list entry it already had - the profile path replaces it, so there was nothing left to print. The request asks for the title now, and a test pins it.

entries.title: The AniList button stops stretching across the page
entries.detail: When a title had nothing to add - a show you are already tracking, or one opened from your activity - the action row drew a single bordered button the full width of the screen, which reads as the page's main call to action rather than as one of two controls. It takes half the row when it shares it, and its natural width when it is alone.

entries.title: Your score, in the artwork header
entries.detail: The score was half a page down in the Details card, between Source and Popularity, while the header already answered how long a title is, what it is and whether it is out. It now sits in the same chip row as a percentage.

entries.title: Back works after tapping twice
entries.detail: Tapping the profile button, the gear, a face in a profile's Social tab or the tier list twice in a row pushed a second copy of the same screen onto the back stack. Every copy looks identical, so Back appeared to do nothing until the duplicates ran out, and each one held a ViewModel and its own scroll position alive behind it. Those hops are single-top now: a repeat tap is a no-op.

entries.title: Settings tabs move
entries.detail: Switching between Info, Theme and Edit replaced the page in a single frame, so a tap on the tab bar looked like nothing had happened until the heading was read. The three cross over on the shared springs, and the refresh-interval chips and the reset button no longer snap: their colours and border spring, and the reset row grows into place.

entries.title: A refresh no longer jerks the profile
entries.detail: The spinner that appears while a profile reloads popped into existence and shoved every tab down by its own height, then vanished and pulled them back. It now springs open and shut, and a library grid slides its posters to their new cells when you change the type, filter, sort or search instead of redrawing them in place.
